passage: The small library above the Nandgaon post office had two keepers who could not agree. Ramesh Kaka wanted the old ledger, the same shelves and the same closing bell at six. Elizabeth, back from college, wanted a comic corner, floor cushions and a new layout every month. Each called the other's idea "nonsense" behind their back. Seema, twenty and on the evening shift, asked Ramesh Kaka what the ledger kept safe. "Every borrower's name for forty years. Nobody's book gets lost." She asked Elizabeth what the cushions were for. "The girls from the bus stand. They won't come in if it feels like an office." Seema set the ledger on the new counter and put the cushions beside the history shelf. Both keepers grumbled, and then both stayed late.

qa.q: What did Ramesh Kaka say the ledger kept safe?
qa.a: Every borrower's name for forty years, so nobody's book gets lost.

qa.q: What does Seema asking each keeper what their idea was for suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She seems curious rather than irritated by the quarrel, wanting to understand what each preference protected instead of writing either one off as nonsense.

qa.q: Which choice did Seema make with the ledger and the cushions, and why did it work?
qa.a: She kept the ledger on the new counter and put cushions by the history shelf, so both the old trust and the new readers were served.

qa.q: How might the girls from the bus stand see the library after the change?
qa.a: They may find it less like an office and more welcoming, while their borrowing is still kept safe in the ledger.

grounding: A young woman sees value in both a traditional and a novelty-loving keeper by asking what each preference protects, instead of labelling either.

passage: "He's so dull," Dalia whispered, as Tomasz taped the paper cleaning rota back on the fridge for the third time. "And she's so flighty," Tomasz muttered later, when Dalia proposed a different cuisine for every Sunday dinner. Amara, twenty-one and sharing the Manchester flat with both, had nearly agreed with each of them. Instead, over tea, she asked Tomasz what the paper rota gave him. "Nobody argues about who did the bins. It's all there." She asked Dalia what the new dishes gave her. "Home was the same four meals for twenty years. This feels like breathing." That Sunday the rota stayed on the fridge, and the pot held Dalia's peanut stew. Tomasz took seconds.

qa.q: Where did Tomasz tape the cleaning rota?
qa.a: He taped the paper cleaning rota back on the fridge.

qa.q: What does Amara nearly agreeing with each flatmate, then asking questions instead, suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She seems torn between them at first, then curious, wanting to know what each preference gave them rather than calling them "dull" or "flighty".

qa.q: What choice at the turning point let both flatmates' needs fit together?
qa.a: Amara let the paper rota stay while Dalia cooked something new, so order and novelty both had a place.

qa.q: What might Dalia feel when Tomasz takes seconds of her stew?
qa.a: She may feel accepted instead of judged as flighty, and see that he can enjoy something new when his order is respected.

grounding: A young woman refuses to label one flatmate dull and the other flighty and asks what each one's preference protects.

passage: The fest committee room in the college's old block was getting loud. 'Same stalls, same lamp-lighting, same quiz, every year since 1998,' Farhan said. 'It's a museum.' Bidisha's jaw set. 'And your plan is a DJ and a hundred random things nobody asked for.' Maria, chairing her first meeting, felt the room tighten. She held up a hand. 'Wait. Bidisha, what does the old format protect for you?' Bidisha paused. 'Alumni come back because they know exactly where the quiz will be. First-years feel they've joined something.' 'Farhan, what does your change protect?' 'The students who never feel the old stuff is theirs. Hostel kids from other states, mostly.' Maria wrote both lists on the board. Neither was dull; neither was shallow. By six they had kept the lamp-lighting and the quiz, and handed Farhan the evening.

qa.q: Which two things did the committee keep from the old format?
qa.a: The lamp-lighting and the quiz.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling as the argument grew louder?
qa.a: She felt the tension in the room and was probably nervous chairing her first meeting, yet calm enough to ask each side a question.

qa.q: Why did Maria's question about what each format protects work?
qa.a: It turned labels like 'museum' into real reasons, alumni belonging and outsiders feeling included, so both could be honoured.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt on being asked what the old format protects?
qa.a: Bidisha, who had felt mocked, probably felt taken seriously and calmer, able to explain rather than defend.

grounding: Shows a young adult who, faced with a very traditional and a very open classmate, asks what each preference protects instead of labelling either.

passage:
Dear Vishal,
I keep thinking about our fight in the mess, when I called your life 'a timetable with legs'. That was unkind, and I'm sorry.
Here's what I've worked out since. You go home every second weekend, you eat the same dal, you've been in the same study group since first year. I used to think that meant you were afraid of the world. Then I asked myself what it protects. Your amma, who lives alone now. Your marks, which your scholarship depends on. Friendships that actually last.
You once called me shallow for changing clubs four times. Maybe ask what my changes protect too: I'm still looking for the thing I'm good at.
Chai on Friday? Your usual place. I won't complain about the menu.
Tenzin

qa.q: What did Tenzin once call Vishal's life?
qa.a: 'A timetable with legs'.

qa.q: How does Tenzin feel about the fight in the mess now?
qa.a: Tenzin feels sorry and a bit ashamed, seeing the remark as unkind now that the reasons behind Vishal's routines are clear.

qa.q: What question helped Tenzin change, and how could Vishal use it too?
qa.a: Asking what a habit protects; Vishal could ask it about Tenzin's club-switching and see a search for strengths rather than shallowness.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Vishal would probably feel relieved and respected, since the letter names real reasons for the routines, and might happily accept Friday's chai.

grounding: Shows a young adult who comes to value a more traditional friend's routines by asking what they protect, and stops labelling caution as dull.

passage: Honestly, the first time Irfan told me he was quitting engineering for pottery, I called him flaky. To his face. I'm Seema, the practical cousin, and I thought I was helping. Then that same month Nani refused to change a single dish at Eid. Same biryani, same sheer khurma, same order of serving. Irfan called her stuck. And I thought, hang on, I just did that to him. So I asked Nani why the dishes mattered. She said, 'These are the ones your Nana cooked with me.' It was memory, not stubbornness. Then I asked Irfan what pottery gave him. He said it was the first thing that made his hands and his head quiet together. I'm not saying everyone is right about everything. I'm saying I ask the question now, before I reach for the label.

qa.q: What did Nani say about the Eid dishes?
qa.a: 'These are the ones your Nana cooked with me.'

qa.q: How did Seema feel on hearing Irfan call Nani stuck?
qa.a: Seema felt uncomfortable and a little guilty, recognising the same labelling Seema had just used on Irfan.

qa.q: What habit has Seema built, and why does it help?
qa.a: Asking what a choice means to someone before labelling it; it uncovered memory behind Nani's dishes and calm behind Irfan's pottery.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when asked why the dishes mattered instead of being called stuck?
qa.a: Nani probably felt respected and understood, able to share a memory of Nana instead of defending a rule.

grounding: Shows a young adult who learns to ask what both a very open cousin and a very traditional grandmother are protecting, instead of labelling either.

passage: I play bass in our college band, so I've watched this up close. I'm Siddharth. Last month, Farhan wanted to play only old ghazals, exactly as recorded. Neha wanted to remix everything with electronic beats. They'd started calling each other "boring uncle" and "attention seeker." Lakshmi, our singer, didn't pick a side. I don't know what she was thinking, but I saw what she did. She asked Farhan, "What does keeping the old songs pure protect for you?" He said his late grandfather sang them. Then she asked Neha what the remixes meant to her. Neha said she wanted younger people to hear them. Lakshmi said, "So you both want the songs to live." They agreed on one pure ghazal and one remix. The labels stopped.

qa.q: What instrument does Siddharth play?
qa.a: Bass.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel watching Lakshmi handle the argument?
qa.a: Siddharth seemed impressed and relieved, noticing how she calmed things without taking sides.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do that respected both styles?
qa.a: She asked each person what their preference protected, found their shared goal and avoided labelling either as dull or shallow.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt when Lakshmi asked about the old songs?
qa.a: He may have felt respected and understood, able to share that his late grandfather sang them.

grounding: An observer describes a young adult who respects both traditional and very open styles, asking what each protects and avoiding labels.
